In extreme situations, some people experience tonic immobility, an involuntary, temporary paralysis: in a study of 298 women seen at an emergency clinic after sexual assault, 70% reported significant tonic immobility during the assault (Möller et al., 2017). And researchers have proposed that stress responses, particularly in women, include patterns of tending and befriending, protecting others and seeking social support, alongside fight-or-flight (Taylor et al., 2000).

This matters for two reasons. First, no one should ever be blamed for freezing; it is a normal biological response, not a failure of character or training. Second, it shows that the body under threat is not a simple machine that executes its programming. It has many possible responses, and the one that emerges depends on context, history, and the brain’s ability to shift between them. Training can shape that ability. It cannot guarantee it.

Danger three, revisited: invisible variables

My list ends with “real-world variables (weapons, multiple threats, legal aftermath).” Each of these deserves a sentence.

Weapons can be hidden, and anxiety can lead people to act on expectations of a threat rather than on what is actually there (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2012). Multiple threats mean that a practitioner locked into one person may be exposed to others. Legal aftermath is real: in most legal systems, the force a person uses in self-defence must be necessary and proportionate, and a response that would have been justified at one level of threat may be a serious crime at another (Chapter 11). There is a fourth variable the list does not mention: the other person may not be a threat at all.

What the warning teaches

My own conclusion is the right one: “Mastery requires not only technical perfection but profound self-knowledge and emotional regulation.” Research suggests one more ingredient. Self-knowledge and emotional regulation must themselves be trained, and trained into the same automatic layers as the techniques, because under stress the automatic layers are what remain. The next two chapters describe how.

⚠ Caution

If you have trained a one-setting response, add settings. If your practice has built a reflex of full-force chains, do not test it on the street. Begin the brake drills of Chapter 11, slowly and with supervision, and give yourself months. A reflex is not a character. It can be retrained.

No Opponent, No Enemy

Chapter 10

Violence becomes an elegant geometric inevitability rather than a tragic necessity. — from the System of Inevitability source materials, describing the “No Opponent” state

The sentence above is the most important one in the source materials, and the most dangerous. It is honest about its own consequence: the materials add that the No Opponent state “removes natural psychological brakes.” This chapter explains, with some of the most robust research in social psychology, why those brakes matter and how they can be removed. Then it proposes a different reading of “no opponent,” one that keeps everything valuable in the idea and leaves the danger behind.

How good people do harm

The psychologist Albert Bandura spent decades studying a puzzle: how ordinary people, with ordinary moral standards, come to do harmful things without feeling that they are betraying those standards. His answer was moral disengagement. Moral standards regulate behaviour only when they are activated, and there are many psychological manoeuvres by which people switch them off (Bandura et al., 1996; Bandura, 1999). The manoeuvres he identified include:

  • moral justification: reframing harm as serving a worthy purpose;
  • sanitizing language: describing harm in neutral or technical terms;
  • advantageous comparison: making harm look small beside something worse;
  • displacement and diffusion of responsibility: “I was ordered to,” “everyone did it,” “it just happened”;
  • minimizing or disregarding the consequences of one’s actions;
  • blaming and dehumanizing the people who are harmed.

These are not exotic. They are everyday thought patterns, and they predict real behaviour. A meta-analysis of 27 samples including 17,776 children and adolescents found a consistent positive relationship between moral disengagement and aggressive behaviour (Gini et al., 2014).

● Evidence: well-established

Moral disengagement enables harm. People can disengage their moral standards from harmful conduct through justification, sanitizing language, displacement of responsibility, minimizing consequences, and dehumanization (Bandura et al., 1996; Bandura, 1999). Moral disengagement is consistently associated with aggression in children and youth (Gini et al., 2014).

People as shapes

Dehumanization, perceiving others as less than fully human, comes in more than one form. In an influential review, Nick Haslam distinguished an “animalistic” form, which denies people uniquely human qualities such as refinement and reason, from a “mechanistic” form, which denies them the warmth and emotion of human nature and represents them as objects or automata. He argued that dehumanization is not only a feature of war and genocide but an everyday social phenomenon, rooted in ordinary thinking (Haslam, 2006; Haslam & Loughnan, 2014).

A striking series of experiments found that dehumanization does not increase all kinds of violence. It increases instrumental violence, harm done to achieve some other goal, but not violence that perpetrators see as morally righteous. Using dehumanizing rather than humanizing language made participants more willing to harm strangers for money, and participants spontaneously dehumanized strangers when they imagined harming them for money (Rai et al., 2017).

Now read the source materials again with these findings in mind. The other person becomes a set of nodes. Contact is a “latch.” Joints are “compromised.” Violence is a “geometrical resolution,” an “inevitability,” something the system does rather than something the practitioner chooses. The outcome “feels predestined rather than chosen.”

This is, almost point for point, the vocabulary of moral disengagement: sanitizing language (resolution, compromise, overlay), displacement of responsibility (the system controls the outcome), and mechanistic dehumanization (the opponent as geometry). I do not intend harm, and the materials themselves flag the danger. But a philosophy that renders violence “elegant” and “inevitable” is giving its practitioners exactly the psychological tools that research shows make harm easier.

◐ Evidence: suggestive · emerging

The language of inevitability resembles the language of disengagement. This is my analysis, based on established research (Bandura, 1999; Haslam, 2006; Rai et al., 2017). No study has examined the System of Inevitability’s language or its effects on practitioners.

What martial arts culture can do

The culture of a training community matters. Book 2 reviewed this evidence in detail. In one classic study, teenage boys taught traditional Tae Kwon Do, with its psychological and philosophical teachings, became less aggressive, while those taught a “modern” version without those teachings became more aggressive (Trulson, 1986). In intervention studies with young people, martial arts training reduced aggression (Harwood et al., 2017), while other meta-analytic evidence finds no benefit or even harm, especially with intense training (Gubbels et al., 2016). A school-based Tae Kwon Do programme improved children’s self-regulation and prosocial behaviour (Lakes & Hoyt, 2004). The same physical techniques can make people gentler or harsher, depending on what is taught alongside them.

In policing, researchers have compared a “warrior” mindset, in which officers see themselves as fighting crime, with a “guardian” mindset, in which they value working with the public. Survey data from two police departments found that these are distinct but related orientations, and that the guardian mindset was associated with placing greater priority on communication during encounters with citizens (McLean et al., 2020). Book 2 also described a randomized evaluation in which de-escalation training was followed by substantial reductions in use-of-force incidents and in injuries to both citizens and officers (Engel et al., 2022).

● Evidence: well-established

Culture shapes what technique becomes. Martial arts training can reduce or increase aggression depending on how and in what culture it is taught (Trulson, 1986; Harwood et al., 2017; Gubbels et al., 2016). A guardian orientation in policing is associated with prioritizing communication (McLean et al., 2020), and de-escalation training was followed by fewer use-of-force incidents and injuries (Engel et al., 2022).

From no opponent to no enemy

There is a version of “no opponent” that is profound and beautiful. It is found in many contemplative and martial traditions, and it resembles the self-transcendence described in Chapter 7. In it, the practitioner does not hate. They do not need to prove anything. Fear and ego are quiet. The person in front of them is not an enemy to be destroyed but a human being in a difficult moment, perhaps frightened, drunk, desperate, or mistaken.

This version dissolves enmity, not personhood. It removes hatred, not responsibility. And far from removing the brakes, it makes them stronger, because it is much easier to stop striking a person you see as human than a shape you see as a node.

Here is the distinction this book proposes:

No opponent (as written) No enemy (as proposed)
What dissolves Ego, fear, hesitation, moral calculation Ego, fear, hatred, the need to win
What remains Geometry, inevitability The other person; your choice
Who decides “The system controls the outcome” You do, every moment
Force Total, terminal The least that is necessary
Afterward Resolution Care, accountability, reflection

Re-humanizing practice

Compassion can be trained. Short-term compassion training increased how much money people chose to redistribute to a victim of unfairness (Weng et al., 2013), and compassion training strengthened positive feelings in the face of others’ suffering (Klimecki et al., 2013). Neuroscientists distinguish compassion, a warm concern for another’s welfare, from empathic distress, which can lead to withdrawal (Singer & Klimecki, 2014). A compassionate practitioner does not have to collapse in distress at another’s pain, and does not have to stop seeing it.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

Re-humanizing practices (my suggestions).

  • Change the words. Describe your training in human terms. Not “node,” but “his wrist.” Not “resolution,” but “injury.” Not “inevitable,” but “what I chose.”
  • Give your imagined partner a face. In solitary forms, sometimes imagine a specific, real person you would never want to harm, and practise controlling without injuring them.
  • Remember the afterward. At the end of a session, spend one minute imagining the moments after a real encounter: the other person’s family, the police interview, your own feelings the next morning.
  • Practise the compassion meditation of Chapter 7 regularly.

My own phrase deserves to be turned around. Violence is never an “elegant geometric inevitability.” At its very best, it is a tragic necessity, which is exactly why every skilled person should spend a lifetime making it less necessary.

Training the Brake

Chapter 11

The system solves “stopping short” by making stopping short almost impossible. — from the System of Inevitability source materials, listing a danger of the system

This is the most practical chapter in the book, and the one the series has been building toward. Its argument is simple. If a skill can be made automatic, so can the ability to stop it. The brake is not the opposite of mastery. It is part of it.

The brain has a brake

Cognitive scientists study stopping with a simple laboratory task. People respond quickly to a “go” signal, and on some trials a “stop” signal appears shortly afterward, telling them to withhold the response. Gordon Logan and William Cowan proposed that what happens next is a race: the stop signal starts a stopping process that races against the processes driving the ongoing action. If stopping wins, the action is inhibited; if the action wins, it runs to completion (Logan & Cowan, 1984). This stop-signal paradigm has become one of the most widely used tools for studying how behaviour is controlled (Verbruggen & Logan, 2008).

Brain research has identified a network, centred on a region of the right inferior frontal cortex together with circuits through the basal ganglia, that its leading researchers describe as best characterized as a brake. Importantly, this brake can be applied in different ways: totally, to suppress a response outright, or partially, to pause it; and it can be triggered externally, by a stop signal or something salient, or internally, by one’s own goals (Aron et al., 2014).

Two lessons follow for martial practice. First, stopping is a race, and the further a movement has progressed, and the more strongly it is driven, the harder it is to win. Second, the brake has settings. A full stop and a partial pause are both available, and both can be cued from outside or inside.

● Evidence: well-established

Stopping is a trainable race. Response inhibition is modelled as a race between stopping and going (Logan & Cowan, 1984; Verbruggen & Logan, 2008). A frontal–basal-ganglia network acts as a brake that can stop an action totally or pause it partially, cued from outside or by internal goals (Aron et al., 2014).

Why the brake must be automatic too

Chapter 3 showed that stress shifts behaviour toward habit, and Chapter 9 that it can tilt decisions toward harm. A brake that depends on slow, deliberate reflection is likely to fail exactly when it is most needed. The brake therefore has to be built into the same layers as the techniques: rehearsed thousands of times, in context, under gradually increasing pressure, until stopping is as natural as starting.

There is good evidence that pressure-specific practice helps. In police training, officers who practised shooting against an opponent who could fire back no longer performed worse under that pressure, while a comparison group did; the benefit was still present four months later (Oudejans, 2008; Nieuwenhuys & Oudejans, 2011). Officers who received training in physiological control during stressful incidents made more correct use-of-force decisions in realistic scenarios (Andersen & Gustafsberg, 2016). Self-defence training that rehearsed complete violent situations, including the moments before physical contact, improved officers’ communication, proportionality, and control (Renden et al., 2017).

There is also a sobering limit. In the study described in Chapter 9, three weeks of practice did not remove the effect of threat on officers’ mistaken decisions to shoot (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2015). Brakes take a long time to build, and no brake is perfect. That is one more reason to avoid situations in which one is needed.

The brake drills

The following drills are my suggestions, drawn from the research above. They are designed to be practised slowly at first, and with a qualified partner or coach where partner work is involved.

1. Stop on cue (solo)

At the dummy or the bag, perform a flowing sequence at slow speed. Have a phone app or a recording give random audio cues. On the cue, freeze completely and hold for one breath, then step back. Over weeks, raise the speed. Keep a log of how often you stop cleanly and how far each movement travels after the cue (Appendix A). Then add a second cue meaning pause, a partial stop, followed by continuing softly. You are training both settings of the brake.

2. Touch, don’t strike

On the bag or dummy, deliver every technique as a light touch that stops at the surface. Then at one centimetre short. Then, occasionally, at a half-power target. The goal is not to remove power but to make the amount of power a choice. The source materials say there is no “light touch”; this drill builds one.

3. The proportionality ladder

Picture a ladder of responses, each one more forceful than the last:

  1. Leave, or create distance.
  2. Speak: calm, clear, firm.
  3. Signal: open hands, a fence, a barrier posture.
  4. Free yourself from a grab, without striking.
  5. Control without injury.
  6. Strike, only to create an opening to escape.
  7. Stop, as soon as the threat stops.

In solitary practice, rehearse each rung on its own. In partner practice, the partner (at a pre-agreed, safe intensity) presents a scenario, and you respond with the lowest rung that would work, then step back. Most of your repetitions should be on the lower rungs, because most of life is.

4. The release

Whenever the system’s “latch” engages in training, whether a trap, a lock, or a wrap, practise letting go on a cue from your partner. Then practise letting go without a cue, as soon as your partner relaxes. Releasing should become as automatic as engaging. This is the antidote to the “irreversible” attachment the source materials describe.

5. The first words

In partner scenarios, begin every encounter with words, not hands. Practise a few calm sentences until they are automatic: “I don’t want any trouble.” “Let’s both step back.” “I’m leaving now.” The first words of an encounter shape what follows; this is part of what modern de-escalation training teaches (Engel et al., 2022).

6. Restraint imagery

Each day, rehearse in imagination one realistic scenario in which you choose a low rung, or leave (Chapter 5). Imagery of successful performance under threat helped officers preserve their performance (Colin et al., 2014). Make the successful performance a restrained one.

7. Pressure, gradually

When the drills are reliable at low intensity, raise the pressure gradually: more speed, more noise, a little fatigue (never to the point of degraded form; see Chapter 6), a partner who is louder. Pressure training is what makes skills hold under pressure (Oudejans, 2008). It is what will make the brake hold too.

⚠ Caution

Partner work must be controlled. Agree on intensity, a tap-out signal, and a stop word before every session. Never practise locks or breaks on a partner at speed. Have a qualified instructor present for any partner work involving joints or strikes. The point of partner practice in this chapter is control, not victory.

The law, in general terms

This book cannot give legal advice, and the law varies widely between countries and states. But some broad principles are common to many legal systems, and every practitioner should know them in general terms and learn the specifics where they live.

  • Necessity. Force in self-defence is generally permitted only when it is necessary to prevent a threatened harm.
  • Imminence. The threat generally has to be present or immediately about to happen, not a past wrong or a future possibility.
  • Proportionality and reasonableness. The force used is generally expected to be reasonable in proportion to the threat. In the United States, for example, the Supreme Court held in 1989 that police use of force must be judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene (as described by Klinger & Brunson, 2009); civilian standards differ by state.
  • When the threat ends, the force must end. Continuing to strike someone who is no longer a threat is generally no longer self-defence.
  • Retreat. Some jurisdictions expect a person to retreat when it is safely possible; others do not.
  • Training can be held against you. In some legal systems, a trained person’s actions may be judged differently because of what they knew and could do.

A system that makes “stopping short almost impossible” is, in these terms, a legal danger as well as a moral one. Learn the law where you live from a qualified source.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

The law is not a brake on its own. The legal principles above are general and not legal advice. They are included because the source materials themselves list “legal aftermath” as a danger, and because the habits trained in this chapter (necessity, the least force, stopping when the threat ends) are the habits most legal systems expect.

How to Test the Philosophy

Chapter 12

Let the claim be beautiful. Then let it be tested. — Cory Snell

Every book in this series ends its practical section with the same invitation: if a claim matters, test it. This chapter designs simple, honest tests for the philosophy of the System of Inevitability, especially its most extraordinary claims: that a practitioner’s presence calms others, that contact “latches,” and that the system “completes” other arts. It also designs tests for the qualities this book has argued matter most: the brake, proportionality, and calm.

None of these tests has been run. They are my proposals. Anyone is invited to improve them, run them, and publish the results, positive or negative.

Why testing matters

We are poor judges of ourselves. People who perform poorly often overestimate their performance, partly because the skills needed to do well are the skills needed to recognize doing well (Kruger & Dunning, 1999). Expectation changes outcomes. Placebo effects have been reported across many sports (Beedie & Foad, 2009). Measurements wobble. Any measure varies from day to day, and real change must be distinguished from that noise (Hopkins, 2000). And a practitioner who sees people grow calm around them may be noticing the times it happens and forgetting the times it does not.

None of this means the experiences are false. It means they need checking by methods that protect us from our own hopes.

● Evidence: well-established

Self-assessment is unreliable; expectation matters. People tend to overestimate their own competence (Kruger & Dunning, 1999). Expectations can produce placebo effects on sports performance (Beedie & Foad, 2009). Measures need to be reliable enough to detect real change (Hopkins, 2000).

Test 1: Does calm presence spread?

Claim: “In casual encounters, people experience an inexplicable sense of calm, clarity, or grounded safety.”

A simple version. Recruit volunteers who do not know the purpose of the study. Each spends a few minutes in a neutral, structured activity (a short conversation from a script, say, or a shared puzzle) with a partner. Some partners are long-term practitioners; others are matched non-practitioners of similar age, sex, and manner. Neither the volunteers nor the person collecting the data know which partner is which. Afterward, volunteers rate how calm, safe, and at ease they feel, on standard scales, before and after. Others’ reports, gathered blind, are the heart of the test.

Making it stronger. Add a mildly stressful task (a short public-speaking preparation, for instance) so there is anxiety to calm. Record heart rate and heart-rate variability in both people, following published guidance on measurement (Laborde et al., 2017). Repeat with many practitioners and many non-practitioners, so that the results don’t depend on one charismatic person. Write down the predictions, the measures, and the analysis before collecting any data, so that results cannot be reinterpreted afterward.

What would count. If volunteers reliably feel calmer with practitioners than with matched controls, that is evidence that the practice cultivates a calming presence, which would be a valuable finding. It would not, on its own, show anything about a “field.”

Test 2: Is the calm carried by ordinary channels?

Claim: the calm is carried by “a living toroidal/helical geometric field.”

The ordinary explanation (Chapter 8) is that calm travels through breathing, voice, face, posture, and movement. The two explanations make different predictions. If calm is carried by ordinary channels, it should weaken or disappear when those channels are blocked, and it should be reproducible by non-practitioners who learn to breathe, speak, and move calmly. If it is carried by a field, it should persist when the practitioner is present but unseen and unheard, and the volunteer should not need to know they are there.

A blinded design. A volunteer sits completing a stressful task, with physiological recording. On randomized trials, a practitioner sits silently behind a screen in the same room, or the chair is empty. Neither the volunteer nor the experimenter in the room knows which condition is running; sound masking prevents cues. The prediction of the field claim is that the volunteer becomes calmer on practitioner trials. The prediction of the ordinary explanation is no difference.

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

A fair test of the field claim. This design is my proposal. A null result would not show that calm presence is unreal; it would show that it is carried by ordinary, learnable channels, which is good news, because anyone can learn them.

Test 3: Do two nervous systems synchronize?

Physiological synchrony between people can be measured (Palumbo et al., 2017), and it has been linked to relationship quality in psychotherapy (Tschacher & Meier, 2020). A practitioner and a volunteer could both wear heart-rate monitors during a structured interaction, and synchrony could be compared between practitioner pairs and control pairs. Because two people doing the same task may synchronize simply because they are doing the same task, a careful analysis would compare real pairs with “pseudo-pairs,” recordings from people who were never together. Note that strong effects in past research have mostly appeared between people who are close (Chapter 8).

Test 4: Does the brake work?

This is the most important test, and the easiest to run.

Stop latency and overshoot. Film the stop-on-cue drill of Chapter 11 from the side at a known frame rate, with an audible or visual cue that appears in the video. Measure the time from cue to complete stop, and how far the hand or foot travels after the cue. Repeat monthly. Improvement means the brake is getting faster.

Stop under pressure. Repeat the measurement with added pressure: more speed, noise, mild fatigue, an unpredictable partner. Pressure-specific training is what makes skills hold under pressure (Oudejans, 2008), so this is where the brake is really tested.

Clean release. In controlled partner work, measure the time from a partner’s release signal to the moment the practitioner fully lets go.

Test 5: Proportionality

Using scenarios like those of Chapter 11, have a trained partner present a range of situations, from mild to serious, in random order. Have qualified observers who do not know the practitioner’s training history rate each response for proportionality and control on a simple five-point scale, a method like the one used to assess police self-defence skills (Nieuwenhuys et al., 2009). A practitioner who meets mild scenarios with mild responses is showing the brake at work. One who meets every scenario with the same full-force chain is showing exactly the danger I warned of.

Test 6: Does the overlay “complete” other arts?

Claim: “Any technique or movement becomes more efficient, structurally inevitable, and injury-resistant once the geometric overlay is applied.”

This is the broadest claim in the materials, and the hardest to test as stated. A fair version would pick one specific skill (a particular throw, a sprint start, a golf swing), recruit people who already practise it, randomly assign half to learn the overlay and half to an equal amount of ordinary extra practice, and measure performance and injuries afterward. Research on transfer suggests caution in advance: skills tend to transfer to closely related tasks, and far transfer is rare (Barnett & Ceci, 2002; Sala & Gobet, 2017).

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

“It completes them.” The universal-overlay claim is untested. It may contain a real insight, that attention to smooth, curved, whole-body movement can improve many activities, but “every technique” and “structurally inevitable” are not claims evidence can currently support.

A summary of tests

Claim or quality Test What would support it
Calm presence Blinded volunteer ratings with practitioners vs matched controls Calmer ratings with practitioners
“Geometric field” Practitioner unseen and unheard behind a screen, randomized Calmer physiology on practitioner trials
Co-regulation Paired heart-rate recording vs pseudo-pairs More synchrony in real pairs
The brake Filmed stop latency and overshoot, with and without pressure Fast, clean stops that hold under pressure
Proportionality Blind expert ratings across mild and serious scenarios Responses scaled to the scenario
Universal overlay Randomized trial in one specific skill Better performance or fewer injuries than equal extra practice

What a good result looks like

The most hopeful outcome of all these tests is not proof of a field or an inevitable lock. It is a practitioner who is measurably calm, whose presence helps others feel safe, who can stop any movement on a cue, who meets mild provocations with mild responses, and who can say, honestly, “I chose.” That would be a result worth sharing.

Inevitability, Reconsidered

Chapter 13

The space between a cue and a response is small. Practice can make it wider. — Cory Snell

The System of Inevitability begins with a boy waxing a car. It ends, in its own telling, with “a deep sense of predestined resolution.” Between those two points lies one of the most interesting ideas in martial practice: that the movements of everyday life can become the training ground for a whole art, that skill can be so complete it no longer needs a partner, and that a practitioner’s calm can be felt by others.

This book has tried to honour that idea, and to tell the truth about it.

What the science supports

Much of the system’s foundation is sound. Skills really can be learned without explicit rules (Chapter 2). Practice woven into daily life can work (Clemson et al., 2012). Habits really do form through repetition in context, and they really do become the default (Chapter 3). Human movement really does have lawful, curved, smooth geometry (Chapter 4). Imagined practice really does engage the motor system and improve performance, modestly (Chapter 5). The self really can grow quiet, and when it does, people often become kinder (Chapter 7). Calm and stress really do pass between people, through face, voice, breath, posture, and the rhythms of the body (Chapter 8).

What the science questions

Other parts of the system are untested, and some are contradicted by what we know. There is no evidence for an energetic field, for anxious “frequencies,” or for an irreversible latch on others’ minds. The Venus flytrap, the fight-ending strike, and the universal overlay have never been examined. And the deepest part of the philosophy, the state in which “the practitioner no longer controls the system,” turns out to be a familiar psychological condition, the dominance of habit under stress, which research associates not with wisdom but with narrowed choices, distorted perception, and decisions tilted toward harm (Chapter 9).

What I saw

It is worth saying again: I saw this. The source materials list the dangers plainly. They say the system “removes natural psychological brakes.” They warn that de-escalation becomes improbable, that real-world variables can be underestimated, and that solitary intensity can turn the system’s power against the practitioner’s own body. And they end with a sentence that could stand as the motto of this whole series: “Mastery requires not only technical perfection but profound self-knowledge and emotional regulation.”

This book has simply tried to take that sentence seriously, and to show what research says self-knowledge and emotional regulation require.

The upgrade

The series these books belong to was written in the hope of contributing, in some small way, to an upgrade in human consciousness. What would that mean here?

It would not mean a mind that acts without choosing. It would mean a mind in which choosing has become as fluent as acting: in which pausing, scanning, speaking softly, releasing, and stopping are as automatic as any strike. Not “no opponent,” in the sense of no person. No enemy, in the sense of no hatred. Ego quiet, fear quiet, and conscience awake.

That is, perhaps, the real inevitability worth training for. Not that every contact ends in a lock. But that every contact, every encounter, every ordinary moment of reaching, turning, stirring, and carrying, becomes a small rehearsal of care: the hand that moves smoothly, and can stop; the presence that is calm, and invites rather than captures; the person who is skilled, and chooses gently.

Wax on, wax off

Return, for a moment, to the scene where all of this began. A boy is frustrated by chores that seem to have nothing to do with fighting. He discovers that they have been training him all along. The lesson most people remember is that practice can be hidden in ordinary life.

There is a second lesson in the same story, easy to miss. The skill the boy learns is taught to him by someone who has already learned restraint, and the teaching includes when not to fight. Whatever the geometry, the teacher is the one who decides what it is for.

Every practitioner becomes, sooner or later, their own teacher. The question this book leaves with you is the question it began with. Not “How powerful is what I have automated?” but:

What have I automated, and does it include the ability to choose?

○ Practitioner experience · philosophy

A closing practice (my suggestion). Tomorrow, choose one ordinary movement (opening a door, setting down a cup, reaching for a hand) and make it, for one day, a practice of care. Move smoothly. Pause before you finish. Notice the other people around you. That is the whole system, in miniature: everyday geometry, calm presence, and a choosing mind.

Appendix A · Practices and Logs

Copy or print these pages. Fill them in honestly. Film what you can. The point of a log is to let your future self see what your present self cannot.

The daily practices, in brief

  • Everyday geometry (Chapter 2): one ordinary chore a day, done with smooth, curved, unhurried movement.
  • The interrupted figure-eight (Chapter 4): trace slowly; stop completely at a random moment; continue.
  • The restraint form (Chapter 5): three minutes imagining a tense situation handled calmly, at a low rung.
  • The right kind of quiet (Chapter 7): five minutes of settling, then wishing well to a loved one, a neutral person, and a difficult one.
  • Calm presence (Chapter 8): breathe out, lower and slow the voice, soften shoulders and gaze.
  • Re-humanizing words (Chapter 10): describe training in human terms.
  • The brake drills (Chapter 11): stop on cue, touch-don’t-strike, the proportionality ladder, the release, the first words, restraint imagery, gradual pressure.

Appendix B · The Evidence at a Glance

A summary of the main claims discussed in this book, how strong the evidence is, and where to look. “●” marks well-established findings, “◐” suggestive or emerging ones, and “○” practitioner claims that have not been tested.

Claim Strength Key sources
Skills can be learned implicitly, without explicit rules ● Established Reber, 1967; Masters, 1992; Kal et al., 2013
Training woven into daily routines can work ◐ Suggestive (one strong trial in older adults) Clemson et al., 2012
Habits form through repetition in a consistent context ● Established Lally et al., 2010; Wood & Rünger, 2016
Automatic does not have to mean uncontrollable ● Established (theory) Moors & De Houwer, 2006
Stress shifts behaviour toward habit ● Established Schwabe & Wolf, 2009; Arnsten, 2009
Movement follows lawful geometry (power laws, smoothness) ● Established Lacquaniti et al., 1983; Flash & Hogan, 1985; Huh & Sejnowski, 2015
Mental practice improves performance, modestly ● Established Driskell et al., 1994; Toth et al., 2020
Imagery helps preserve performance under threat ◐ Suggestive (one police study) Colin et al., 2014
Solo forms replace interactive practice ○ Not supported Krabben et al., 2019; Pinder et al., 2011
Load spikes and poor recovery cause injury ● Established Soligard et al., 2016; Meeusen et al., 2013
A “misaligned twist under fatigue” can injure the practitioner ◐ Plausible, untested specifically Chapter 6
Selfless states have measurable brain correlates ◐ Suggestive (small samples) Brewer et al., 2011; Josipovic, 2014
Self-transcendence increases connection and kindness ◐ Suggestive Yaden et al., 2017; Piff et al., 2015
Emotions and stress spread between people ● Established Dimberg et al., 2000; Engert et al., 2014
Close partners co-regulate physiology ● Established Coan et al., 2006; Feldman et al., 2011
A stranger’s calm reliably calms others ◐ Thin evidence Palumbo et al., 2017
A “geometric field,” “frequencies,” or “energetic latch” ○ No evidence Chapter 8
Polyvagal theory explains social safety ◐ Contested Porges, 2007; Grossman, 2023
Venus flytrap: escape “geometrically improbable” ○ Untested Chapter 9
“Every strike is a fight-ender” ○ Untested; single punches can kill Pilgrim et al., 2014
Extreme stress distorts perception and biases decisions ● Established Klinger & Brunson, 2009; Nieuwenhuys et al., 2012
Moral disengagement and dehumanization enable harm ● Established Bandura, 1999; Gini et al., 2014; Rai et al., 2017
Martial arts culture shapes aggression ◐ Mixed evidence Trulson, 1986; Harwood et al., 2017; Gubbels et al., 2016
Response inhibition works as a trainable brake ● Established (lab) Logan & Cowan, 1984; Aron et al., 2014
De-escalation training reduces force and injuries ◐ Suggestive (one strong evaluation) Engel et al., 2022
The universal overlay “completes” every art ○ Untested Chapter 12

Glossary

Automaticity — The quality of a process that runs fast, efficiently, and with little conscious attention. Its features (unintentional, uncontrollable, unconscious, efficient, fast) can be separated.

Co-regulation — A process in which two people form a shared emotional system, each helping to stabilize the other’s arousal.

Default mode network — A set of brain regions, including parts of the medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate cortex, that is typically more active at rest and associated with self-related thought and mind-wandering.

De-escalation — Words, posture, distance, and choices that reduce the intensity of a conflict and the likelihood of violence.

Dehumanization — Perceiving others as less than fully human, either as animal-like or as objects and automata.

Dissociation — A sense of detachment from one’s surroundings, body, or experience, common under acute extreme stress.

Emotional contagion — The tendency to catch others’ emotions, often through automatic mimicry of their faces, voices, and postures.

Flow — A state of complete absorption in a challenging activity, in which self-consciousness fades and action feels effortless.

Goal-directed behaviour — Behaviour guided by its expected outcome, which changes when the outcome is no longer wanted. Contrasted with habit.

Habit — A behaviour triggered automatically by a familiar context, learned through repetition, and relatively insensitive to its current outcome.

Heart-rate variability (HRV) — The beat-to-beat variation in heart rhythm, linked to the regulation of emotion and attention.

Implicit learning — Learning that happens without awareness of what is being learned, or without the ability to state it.

Mental practice / motor imagery — Rehearsing a movement in the imagination without performing it.

Minimum jerk — A model in which the brain plans movements to be as smooth as possible, minimizing the rate of change of acceleration.

Moral disengagement — Psychological manoeuvres by which people switch off their moral standards in relation to harmful conduct.

Mushin — Japanese, “no-mind”: in Zen and the martial traditions, a mind that does not stop or cling.

No enemy — This book’s proposed reading of “no opponent”: the dissolution of hatred and ego, without loss of the other person’s humanity or one’s own responsibility.

Nondual awareness — A contemplative state in which the felt separation between self and world relaxes.

Physiological synchrony — Coordination of bodily signals, such as heart rate, between people.

Polyvagal theory — A theory linking the evolution of the vagus nerve to emotion and social behaviour. Its core premises are strongly contested.

Proportionality — Using force reasonably in proportion to the threat; a principle common to many legal systems and to ethical practice.

Representative design — Designing practice so that it preserves the key information of the real situation in which a skill will be used.

Stop-signal paradigm — A laboratory task for studying response inhibition, in which a signal tells a person to withhold an action already under way.

Tonic immobility — An involuntary, temporary paralysis that can occur under extreme threat.

Two-thirds power law — A relationship between the curvature of a drawn path and the speed at which it is traced: speed falls on tighter curves.

About This Book

Title. Shape and Choice: Everyday Geometry, Calm Presence, and the Science of a Choosing Mind. Book 3 of the Companions to the System of Inevitability.

Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. First edition, November 2026.

Also in this series. Book 1: Walking and Turning: Iron, Spirals, and the Science of a Practicing Mind, on the iron balls, the ring bar, and the brain science of juggling and skill. Book 2: Wave and Return: The Bent Fist, the Figure-Eight, and the Science of a Restrained Hand, on the system’s striking: the bent (J) fist, whole-body wave energy, figure-eight motion, breath, safe progression, testing, and the ethics of restraint. Book 4: Lens and Lattice: Altered Perception, the Internal Arts, and the Science of a Curious Practice, a harm-reduction companion on practising the internal arts with curiosity in altered states, responsibly, and on the science of psilocybin, perception, touch, pattern finding, and integration. Book 5: Nucleus and Orbit: Atoms, Necessity, and the Science of an Interwoven Practice, on the system’s atomism, its 3-6-9 architecture, and its quantum language set beside the real science of atoms, necessity, chaos, the fractal body, and interdependence, tying the series together. The series continues.

About this book. Written by Cory Snell, creator of the System of Inevitability. Descriptions of the System are based on a project document, compiled in November 2026, that consolidates an extended conversation about the system's origin, training, philosophy, and dangers. All practices, drills, tests, stop rules, and ethical guidance in this book are mine, drawn from general psychology, motor-learning, exercise, and violence-prevention science.

Method. Every peer-reviewed study cited was checked against its Crossref record (authors, year, title, journal, volume, pages, DOI), and the specific findings reported were checked against the published abstracts. Where no abstract was available, the study is cited only for what its title and record establish, and no numbers are given. Numbers are reported as the original authors reported them. Where a claim is untested, the text says so. No quotations have been invented; quotations from the source materials are reproduced as written.

Illustrations. The nine plates are original geometric studies created for this book, loosely inspired by the themes of the system’s black-and-white card designs; they are not reproductions of those designs. All diagrams are original schematics. Diagrams marked illustrative show shapes, not data. No figure depicts any real person.

Typography. Set in EB Garamond and Cormorant Garamond, with Inter for labels.

Suggested citation. Snell, C. M. (Comp.). (2026). Shape and choice: Everyday geometry, calm presence, and the science of a choosing mind (Companions to the System of Inevitability, Book 3; 1st ed.). Free edition, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

Not advice. Nothing in this book is medical, psychological, or legal advice. Laws on self-defence and the use of force differ between countries and states.

Corrections. Science moves. If you find an error, or a new study that bears on anything here, please share it, and share a corrected copy under the same license.
